newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO forces collaborate to stem violence.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO forces collaborate to stem violence.

text.p: Israeli and Palestinian security forces were on high alert on Saturday to try to stem the bloodletting after three days of clashes in the West Bank, Gaza Strip and Jerusalem in which 68 people were killed.

The United States expects a meeting between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat will be held "quite soon" to try and end the violence, the State Department said on Friday.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns said the date and venue of the meeting would be announced by the parties themselves. But U.S. sources said it could be held as early as Saturday evening at the Erez checkpoint between Israel and the Gaza Strip.
Israeli and Palestinian security officials met on Friday to discuss ways of calming the situation, said Jibril Rajoub, the Palestinian security chief in the West Bank.
"Both sides agreed that they will try to control the situation," Rajoub told Reuters. He did not elaborate.

Despite similiar pledges on Thursday, gun battles and stone-throwing erupted throughout the West Bank, Gaza Strip and Arab East Jerusalem on Friday, leaving seven Palestinians and three Israelis dead.
Israeli and PLO security forces have increased their presence at likely flashpoints but security experts anticipate flare-ups on Saturday as the dead continue to be buried.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu blamed Palestinian President Yasser Arafat for instigating the violence and demanded he intervene immediately to stop it. Since Wednesday, 54 Palestinians and 14 Israelis have been killed.
"He must personally intervene and stop the incitement -- so it is heard from him," Netanyahu told a news conference on Friday.
Netanyahu said he did not consider his internationally criticised decision to open a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem on Tuesday, which sparked the clashes, a blunder.
He reiterated his contention that Arafat "cynically" used the tunnel as an excuse to stir up Arab passions against Israel and force his government into peace concessions.

"The Palestinian security forces did not start the attacks, the Palestinian Authority did not violate agreements by opening the tunnel or open fire at worshippers in al-Aqsa mosque," Nabil Abu Rdainah, adviser to Arafat, said.
Three Palestinian protesters were killed by Israeli police at al-Aqsa mosque after prayers on Friday.
At a Security Council debate at the United Nations, the United States urged the body to encourage Israel and the Palestinians to revive the Middle East peace process and not to condemn Israel.
The call, by U.S. envoy Madeleine Albright, contrasted with the views of most other speakers, who criticised Israel for opening the tunnel and accused it of delaying peace moves.
Syrian Foreign Minister Farouk al-Shara, in a particularly tough speech, said the Israeli-Palestinian crisis showed the Middle East peace process was dying and accused Israel of trying to destroy it.

The Palestinians killed in the clashes and the issue of Jerusalem will be the focus of Palestinian classrooms when school resumes on Saturday, the Authority said. Schools in Palestinian-ruled areas have been on strike since Thursday.
